study.title: Paid parental leave message construction
study.research_question: Does an economic-security frame produce greater support for paid parental leave than a family-wellbeing frame?
study.provenance: Synthetic course materials. Candidate texts are cached course outputs created with an LLM and lightly edited by the instructor. Ratings and flags are instructor-authored mock annotations. Word counts are calculated from the displayed text. These materials are not evidence from a real pretest or experiment.
study.outcome: Hypothetical policy support on a 0–10 scale after exposure

frame_definitions.economic_security: Support paid parental leave because it protects household income and employment stability during a period of care.
frame_definitions.family_wellbeing: Support paid parental leave because it gives families time for care, recovery, and bonding after a birth or adoption.

mock_rating_instrument.warning: The stored scores are single instructor-authored mock values. A real pretest would collect separate responses from sampled participants and report their distribution.

candidates.text: Paid parental leave helps families keep a reliable income while a parent temporarily steps away from work to care for a new child. A statewide guarantee would reduce the financial penalty attached to taking necessary leave and make continued employment more feasible after a birth or adoption.

No worker should lose financial security for welcoming a child. Twelve weeks of paid leave would protect every participating household from income loss, prevent thousands of job separations each year, and repay the state through higher tax receipts within two years. The proposal would let parents manage a major life transition without choosing between a paycheck and keeping their job.

A period of paid parental leave can keep an interruption for caregiving from becoming a permanent loss of earnings. By replacing part of a worker's wages for twelve weeks, the proposal supports household budgets and makes a return to the same job more realistic.
Paid leave gives parents precious time to welcome a child without immediately returning to work. It can also soften the short-term pressure on a family budget.

The proposed paid-leave guarantee would replace part of an employee's wages during twelve weeks of parental leave. The aim is to make caregiving leave financially possible while preserving the worker's connection to employment.

When unpaid time away is the only option, a new child can produce an abrupt fall in household income. Partial wage replacement during parental leave would give workers a more stable route through the interruption and back into employment.

The first weeks after a birth or adoption are an important period of care and adjustment. Paid parental leave would give families time to recover, form routines, and care for a new child without forcing an immediate return to work.
A baby needs its mother at home during the first months of life. Paid leave would protect that special bond and help mothers devote themselves fully to caring for their newborns.

Paid parental leave gives a family protected time to care for a child and adapt to new responsibilities. That period can support recovery, shared caregiving, and the development of everyday routines before work resumes.

Welcoming a child changes a family's daily life. Twelve weeks of paid parental leave would create time for care, recovery, and bonding during that transition, including for families formed through adoption.

Every child deserves twelve uninterrupted weeks with a parent, and research proves that the proposal would eliminate postnatal stress across the state. Paid leave would give all families calm, secure beginnings and ensure that children enter later life healthier and more attached. It would also transform workplace culture by making every employer fully supportive of caregiving from the first day.

A period of paid leave would let parents focus on a new child's care while the family adjusts to changed routines. The proposal includes birth and adoption and allows caregiving responsibilities to be shared rather than assigned to one parent.
